youtube.description:
From a dot on an oscilloscope in 1958 to machines that trace rays of light sixty times a second.

1967 · The Brown Box plays games on a TV (Ralph Baer, Bill Harrison and Bill Rusch)
1972 · The first home console goes on sale (Magnavox, from Ralph Baer's design)
1976 · Games on swappable cartridges (Jerry Lawson's team at Fairchild; Wallace Kirschner and Lawrence Haskel at Alpex)
1977 · The Atari 2600 (Atari (Jay Miner, Joe Decuir and others))
1983 · The Famicom (Masayuki Uemura's team at Nintendo)
1991 · Nintendo walks away from Sony (Hiroshi Yamauchi (Nintendo); Ken Kutaragi (Sony))

captions.instagram:
How does a PlayStation work?

Sixty times a second, a console reads your thumbs, runs a whole world and paints 8 million pixels, all in 16.7 milliseconds. Open one up in 3D and see how a PlayStation does it, and why it needs so much cooling.

→ A games console is a computer built for one job: drawing a game world 60 times a second.
→ One chip holds an 8-core CPU and the GPU. Round it: 16 GB of memory and a very fast SSD.
→ Read the controller, run the game, draw the picture: the console does all of it in 16.7 milliseconds.
→ Ask for too much and the frame misses its deadline. 60 frames a second drops to 30.
→ Game worlds are made of triangles. The GPU finds which pixels each one covers, then colours them in.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/consoleclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a PlayStation work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Sixty times a second, a console reads your thumbs, runs a whole world and paints 8 million pixels, all in 16.7 milliseconds. Open one up in 3D and see how a PlayStation does it, and why it needs so much cooling.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/consoleclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/consoleclear

In this video:
• A computer built for one job. A games console is a computer with every part chosen in advance.
• One frame every 16.7 milliseconds. Nothing in a game is drawn in advance.
• Triangles into pixels. Game worlds are skins of triangles.
• Why loading got fast. A hard disk must swing an arm to the right track and wait for the platter to turn, thousands of times per level.
• A controller is sensors and motors. Each thumb stick turns two potentiometers, and when their carbon tracks wear the stick drifts.
• 200 watts of heat. Almost all the electricity a console uses becomes heat.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
